title: Praise and blame
hookLine: if others praise or blame the Buddha, the monks should be neither elated nor angry

cards: The first long discourse starts on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda. The Buddha is walking with a large group of monks.

Behind them, on the same road, come two more travelers: a wandering teacher named Suppiya and his young student Brahmadatta. And all the way, they argue. Suppiya is running down the Buddha, his teaching and his monks.
His own student is praising all three. That night everyone stops at the same rest house.

teach.b: Next morning the monks are talking it over: the two of them, one praising and one blaming, all the way down the road.
The Buddha walks in, asks what they're discussing, and gives the instruction that opens the whole long collection.

If others speak against me, or the teaching, or the community, don't be angry or resentful or upset. That would be an obstacle for you. And if you were angry, could you even tell whether what they said was true or false?
The monks admit they couldn't. So if something said is false, calmly explain that it's false: that isn't so, that isn't found among us. Then the other half, easier to miss.
If others speak in praise of me, or the teaching, or the community, don't be elated or delighted or puffed up. That too would be an obstacle.
If what they say is true, simply acknowledge it: yes, that's so, that's found among us. The Pali words are vanna and avanna: praise and dispraise. Notice the symmetry.
Praise is treated as just as risky as blame. Both cloud the mind, and a clouded mind can't check facts. The point isn't to stop caring what's true.

teach.h: STAY LEVEL TO SEE WHAT'S TRUE
teach.b: It's the opposite: stay level, so you can see what's true.
And the monks are told to do it for their own teacher, not just for themselves. Even loyalty is supposed to stay calm.

how: Buddhist teachers across schools speak of the eight worldly winds (gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain), and practitioners train to meet them with equanimity, as the opening of DN 1 describes.

o: a vow of silence before a teacher
anger at being spoken badly of

games.q: praise and blame: tap the pairs.
p: don't be angry; explain what's false
don't be elated; acknowledge what's true

s: the Buddha tells his monks to defend him hotly against critics
he says anger would be an obstacle, and they couldn't even tell what was true.
praise is treated as a risk too
being elated is also an obstacle, so the monks are told not to be puffed up.
the critic and the admirer in the story are teacher and student
Suppiya blames, and his own student Brahmadatta praises.

games.q: you're one of the monks. someone on the road says false things about your teacher. what does DN 1 say to do?
o: stay calm and explain that it isn't so.
games.why: the Buddha says don't be angry, it would cloud you; calmly explain what's false as false: that isn't so, that isn't found among us.

practice: Let a recent compliment play back, and notice the lift in the chest without pushing it away; ask, is it true, part of it, all of it? Then a small criticism: notice the drop, the heat, and ask the same question.
Let both sit side by side, and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Vanna. Praise, with its opposite avanna, dispraise: neither to be angry at nor elated by, so the mind stays clear enough to tell what's true.

orig.note: Pali vanna: praise (also color, appearance); avanna: dispraise. the two winds the monks must meet calmly.

carryVoice: Your line: not elated, not angry. A level mind is the one that can check the facts. Day five hundred twenty-three, done.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (the supreme net), opening section
